---
title: "Why waiting rooms feel longer than they are"
description: "Ten minutes not knowing feels like twenty. Ten minutes with a number and a screen feels like five. The clinic can change the second without touching the first."
image: /assets/social/why-waiting-rooms-feel-longer-og.png
author: "Mesfin Genie"
date: "2026-08-23"
categories: [health, everyday]
---

Nobody enjoys a waiting room. But two waits of the same length can feel
completely different, and the difference is almost never about the clock.

An uncertain wait feels longer than a known one. Being told "about twenty
minutes" makes twenty minutes tolerable; being told nothing makes ten feel
like an insult. An unexplained wait feels longer than an explained one. A
wait alone feels longer than one in company. An unoccupied wait feels longer
than one where you have something to do. And a wait that feels unfair, when
someone who arrived after you goes in first, feels longest of all.

These are old findings from queuing research, and they explain something odd
about healthcare: satisfaction with a clinic tracks the *experience* of
waiting far more closely than the number of minutes. Two practices with
identical waits can sit at opposite ends of a rating scale.

Which means a lot of the fix is cheap. A screen with your position in the
queue. A sentence about why the delay happened. A realistic estimate rather
than an optimistic one. None of these shorten the wait. All of them shorten
how long it feels.

When we ask patients what they will trade for a shorter wait, the answers are
often large. It is worth remembering that some of that value can be delivered
without a single extra appointment slot, by changing the waiting rather than
the wait.
